lead: God renews his covenant with Abraham: he gives Abram and Sarai new names, the sign of circumcision, and the promise of a son, Isaac, though both are old. Abraham falls on his face and laughs. In the Gospel a leper kneels before Jesus and says, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.” Jesus chooses, and touches him. In both readings God keeps his word where human strength has run out, and Psalm 128 sings of the blessing on the house of those who fear the Lord.

r.h: Walk before me, and be blameless
set: Twenty-four years have passed since God first called Abram from Haran (12:4). Ishmael, the son of Hagar, is now thirteen. God appears again and makes the covenant solemn and lasting: Abram becomes Abraham, Sarai becomes Sarah, every male is to be circumcised, and the son of the promise will be born of Sarah within a year. Many scholars think this chapter comes from a priestly tradition in Israel that loved covenants, names and signs. The Lectionary leaves out the verses on the new name of Abraham and the details of the rite.
str: v. 1: God Almighty appears: “walk before me, and be blameless.”
vv. 9–10: Abraham’s side of the covenant: circumcision of every male.
vv. 15–16: Sarai becomes Sarah; she will bear a son and be the mother of nations.
vv. 17–18: Abraham laughs, and prays for Ishmael.
vv. 19–22: the son will be called Isaac; Ishmael too is blessed; the covenant passes through Isaac.
kw: An ancient name of God used to the patriarchs (compare Exodus 6:3). Its exact meaning is uncertain; the Latin translation and later tradition render it “Almighty”. Here it fits: only the Almighty can give a child to a man of ninety-nine and a woman of ninety.
Whole, complete, without defect. The same word is used for an animal fit for sacrifice. God does not ask Abraham for a flawless record but for a whole heart, a life lived entirely before him.
The name means “he laughs”. Abraham laughs here (v. 17), Sarah will laugh at Mamre (18:12), and at the birth Sarah will say, “God has brought laughter for me” (21:6). Doubt becomes joy.
vv: I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless.
The covenant begins with God naming himself, and then with a call. To walk before someone is to live in his sight, as a servant walks before a king.
Every male among you shall be circumcised.
The sign is cut into the body of every family. It marks the people as belonging to God for all generations.
Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed,
He bows in worship and laughs in disbelief at the same moment. God does not withdraw the promise; he names the child after the laughter.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you; I will bless him
Abraham’s prayer for his first son is heard. Ishmael is not the son of the covenant, but he is not forgotten. The name Ishmael means “God hears” (16:11).
ch: The Catechism calls Abraham the model of the obedience of faith, “the father of all who believe” (CCC 145–146), and says that because he walked in God’s presence and in covenant with him he was ready to welcome the mysterious Guest at Mamre (CCC 2571). The Church reads circumcision as a sign that prepared for baptism: Jesus himself was circumcised as a son of Abraham, and his circumcision prefigures the “circumcision of Christ”, which is baptism (CCC 527; Colossians 2:11–12). God’s covenant with Abraham’s descendants remains, for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).

r.h: I do choose. Be made clean!
set: Jesus comes down from the mountain after the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7). Matthew now gathers ten mighty works in chapters 8–9. Having shown Jesus as teacher with authority, he shows him as healer with authority. The first person healed is a man shut out from ordinary life.

Background. The law of Leviticus 13–14 deals with skin diseases that made a person ritually unclean. The Greek word lepra covered several skin conditions, not only what we call leprosy today. The sick person lived apart, and if healed showed himself to the priest and offered the prescribed sacrifice before returning to the community.
str: v. 1: the crowds follow Jesus down from the mountain.
v. 2: the leper kneels: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
v. 3: Jesus stretches out his hand, touches him, and he is cleansed.
v. 4: say nothing; go to the priest; offer the gift Moses commanded.
kw: The word means to bow down in homage, and Matthew uses it for worship of God (4:10) and of Jesus (2:11; 28:9, 17). The leper approaches as one who believes.
The leper does not doubt Jesus’ power, only his will. Jesus answers with the same word: “I do choose.” His will is to heal.
More than healing of the skin: it means restoration to worship and to the community. That is why the man must go to the priest.
vv: Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.
A prayer of complete trust. The man leaves everything to Jesus’ will. Christians have prayed in these words for centuries.
He stretched out his hand and touched him,
Jesus could have healed with a word, as he will for the centurion’s servant. He chooses to touch the one no one touched. Holiness here does not fear contact with impurity; it overcomes it.
go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded,
Jesus respects the law of Moses. The healing is to be confirmed in the proper way, so that the man can take his place again among his people and in worship.
ch: The Catechism speaks of Christ’s compassion towards the sick and his many healings as a sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503), and notes that the sick try to touch him, for power comes from him (CCC 1504). The Church continues his touch in the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, and in every hand stretched out to those whom illness or stigma has set apart. Many missionaries, such as St Damien of Molokai, gave their lives to people with leprosy because of this Gospel.

qa: Why does Jesus tell the man to say nothing to anyone?

In Matthew, as in Mark, Jesus often asks that his mighty works not be spread about. He does not want to be followed as a wonder-worker or a political Messiah. His identity will be fully shown only on the Cross and in the Resurrection. The first duty of the healed man is to go to the priest and give thanks to God.
study: Abraham was told to “walk before me, and be blameless.” What would it mean for me to live this day consciously before God?
Who in my parish or neighbourhood is “untouchable” in practice? How can I stretch out my hand to them?
